implementation_notes: Tokio's oneshot channel is the reply channel: allocate (tx, rx) per request, hand tx to whatever will answer, and await rx wrapped in tokio::time::timeout. The classic correlation table is unnecessary when each request owns its channel, and the runtime's cancellation model does the rest - dropping the timeout future cancels the wait, and dropping tx without sending makes rx resolve to RecvError, the honest replier-gone signal. tower::Service + oneshot is the same mechanism one layer up, and async-nats's client.request() bundles inbox subject plus timeout when a broker is in play.
pitfalls: Dropping the timed-out receive cancels the wait but not the remote work: stopping the replier needs its own cancellation channel or deadline header.
tokio::time::timeout panics when the runtime has no timer enabled (Builder::enable_time/enable_all), so a minimal test runtime fails at the first call.
oneshot::Sender cannot be cloned: for several replies use an mpsc channel plus an explicit completion rule, and drop the sender to signal failure.

variants.name: std::sync::mpsc with recv_timeout (no async runtime)
variants.implementation_notes: Without an async runtime, std::sync::mpsc (or crossbeam-channel) plus recv_timeout gives the blocking form: one channel per request, the worker owns the Sender, and the caller's recv_timeout is the deadline, distinguishing Timeout from Disconnected (worker gone) without any correlation bookkeeping. Use it in thread pools and FFI contexts; the trade is a parked OS thread per outstanding call, so the pool and the number of in-flight requests must be bounded.
pitfalls: Each outstanding call parks a thread: without a bounded pool and request count, request-reply turns into thread exhaustion.
std mpsc is single-consumer: the caller must be the only receiver, and a worker that keeps its Sender after a timeout sends into a channel nobody reads.
